# *"Why Should I Care About Customer Churn?"*

## Customer Churn is Very Important!

### Customer churn = when customers **stop interacting with the business**.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### ~ Low churn ~

 * Low churn is great, customers stay for the long-term and frequently spend.
     * This helps the business actually gain their customer's lifetime value. 
     * Also builds trust and loyalty that makes the business more appealing to new customers.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### ~ High churn ~

 * High churn means people who purchase from the business don't stick around. 
     * We don't get to realise a customer's potential lifetime value if they leave!
     * If the churn is due to poor customer experiences, this might cascade via negative reviews.

:::

::::

### **So customer churn is really bad!**

## Addressing Churn is Easier than Finding New Customers!

\bigskip
\bigskip

### It's usually much cheaper (time, money, effort) to **activate existing customers** than to find new ones!

 * McKinsey & Company estimate the value lost from **losing just 1 existing customer** equates to the value of acquiring **3 new customers** [@downieWhatCustomerChurn2024].

\bigskip
\bigskip
\bigskip

### Of course, new customers are great but keeping them for the long-term is even better!

# *"Okay, So How Do We Measure Customer Churn?"*

## Measuring Customer Churn

\bigskip

### How do we know when a customer has stopped interacting?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
On one extreme, the **exact moment the customer made their most recent purchase** is when they stopped interacting.

 * Any time elapsed after this moment is spend not interacting, so surely they must have churned...

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
On the other extreme, a customer **never can stop interacting** because they could always make a purchase at some point in the future.

 * We don't know when they might interact again, so we can't be sure they've churned.
:::

::::

\bigskip
\bigskip

### Clearly, churn is somewhere between these two extremes...

## Measuring Customer Churn

### The middle ground

 * How many customers stop interacting **within some finite window of time?**

\bigskip

### Churn Rate

$$
C_{\text{rate}} = \left(\frac{\text{\# of Customers who left during time window}}{\text{Total \# of Customers at start of time window}}\right) \times 100
$$

#### What should the time window be?

 * Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly, Annually, etc.
 * It depends on the business model...
     * For instance, a SaaS model might benefit from viewing churn on a monthly basis, since this model offers monthly subscriptions.
